Shilshah
SHIL-shah
n. (a son of Zophah in the genealogy of Asher)
Hebrew Shilshah, might, or possibly the third, from shalosh, three; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:37.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Shilshah is one of six sons listed in a single verse of Asher's register: “Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera” (1 Chronicles 7:37). Their father is named at the head of the sentence: “The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah” (1 Chronicles 7:36), the list running on through the following verse. Eleven sons of one man are named across the two verses, and not one of them has a recorded deed. The Chronicler is working the tribe of Asher down to its fighting strength, which he gives at the end of the section: heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes, numbered twenty and six thousand men. Shilshah is one of the names behind that number. His own name may mean might, or may simply mark him the third. In a register this dense the individual sinks into the total, and that is how an army is counted. The LORD who told Abraham his seed should be as the stars kept the arithmetic by household, and Asher's eleven-son families are part of how the promise was visibly fulfilled.

Key Scripture

1Ch 7:37 — "Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera."

1Ch 7:36 — "The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah,"

1Ch 7:40 — "All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men."

Gen 15:5 — "And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be."

Modern Corruption

Long lists of names are skipped as unreadable; they are the visible arithmetic of a promise that a man's seed would be numberless.

expand to see more

Nobody reads 1 Chronicles 7 for pleasure, and the registers are the part of Scripture most often declared unprofitable. Yet the promise they document is one of the great ones: the LORD brought Abram out and told him to look at the stars and said, So shall thy seed be. The genealogies are what that looked like three hundred years later — one Asherite named Zophah with eleven sons listed, and his tribe mustering twenty-six thousand choice men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps promises in the currency of ordinary households, generation by generation, and writes the receipts down. The believer who skips the lists skips the evidence. Shilshah is one star in the sky Abram was shown.
